analysis.one_liner: Bans imports of semiautomatic assault weapons, large-capacity magazines, and assault-weapon accessories.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Trade Subcommittee in April 1993, it got no hearing, no vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal to bring semiautomatic assault rifles and pistols, detachable magazines holding more than 5 rounds, and accessories like flash suppressors and grenade launchers into the United States. It named specific imported models — AK-47 types, Uzi carbines, HK and FAL types among them — using the tariff schedule as the legal hook, which is why it went to the tax-and-trade committee. Government agencies at the federal, state, and local level could still import these items for official use.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public, if the sponsors' public-safety argument held: fewer foreign-made semiautomatic assault weapons and high-capacity magazines would be available on the U.S. market. Domestic gun makers would also have faced less competition from imported models.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits importation of semiautomatic assault rifles and pistols, including listed AK, Uzi, HK, FAL, and Galil type models [S2][S3].
Bans detachable magazines, belts, or drums holding more than 5 rounds, and parts kits that could be assembled into them [S2][S3].
Bans assault-weapon accessories such as grenade launchers, bayonets, flash suppressors, and night sights [S2][S3].
Carries a stated purpose of providing for the public safety of U.S. citizens [S1][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Importers and dealers of foreign-made semiautomatic rifles and pistols would lose a product line, and buyers who wanted those imported models could no longer purchase them. Lawful government agencies were exempt.

drawbacks.text: The ban covers imports only; domestic manufacturers could still make the same categories of weapons and magazines, limiting the practical effect on availability [S3].

The 5-round magazine threshold is stricter than later federal law (10 rounds), and critics of import bans argue they mostly shift sales to domestic copies rather than reducing the total supply of firearms [S3].
Any type not on the named lists could only be added 'pursuant to law,' so the list risked becoming outdated as new models appeared [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A narrow but real public-safety measure: it targeted a specific slice of the gun market — foreign-made semiautomatic military-style rifles, pistols, and large magazines — while exempting government agencies and leaving domestic production untouched. The cost falls on importers and some buyers; the benefit depends on how much of those weapons' supply came from abroad, which the bill does not address.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee and then to its Trade Subcommittee in early April 1993, and neither ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Sam Gibbons of Florida introduced the bill on March 31, 1993 [S1][S5].
No member joined as a cosponsor [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and on April 2, 1993 to the Subcommittee on Trade [S5].
The subcommittee and full committee took no further action, and the bill died at the end of the 103rd Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms importers and dealers, who kept selling foreign-made semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and high-capacity magazines without the new restrictions. The bill also died despite being sponsored by the Ways and Means chairman himself, showing how little momentum it had.

for.name: Rep. Sam Gibbons
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-FL); sponsor of H.R. 1568 and Chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban imports of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines; it was referred to his own committee, where he did not advance it further.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tariff and trade measures
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Trade Subcommittee on April 2, 1993 and took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Trade
against.role: Ways and Means subcommittee that received the referral
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.role: Firearm owners' lobby opposing restrictions on semiautomatic firearms
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on imported semiautomatic rifles and magazines as part of its broader campaign against the assault-weapons measures considered in 1993-94.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor; the bill never drew a documented party-line fight.

industries.industry: Firearms importers and dealers of foreign-made models
industries.note: The bill would have cut off their supply of imported AK, Uzi, HK, FAL, and similar semiautomatic models plus high-capacity magazines. Their business depended on keeping those imports flowing, against the bill's public-safety aim.

A ban on imported assault weapons would have reduced foreign competition in the same product categories, even though the bill did not restrict domestic production. Domestic makers had no stake in stopping it and could benefit either way.
